newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Senate coup seen curbing investment in Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Senate coup seen curbing investment in Philippines.

text.p: A move by opposition lawmakers to oust the Philippine Senate leader has spooked an already jittery stock market and analysts said on Friday the power struggle among the "Marcos boys" may discourage foreign investment.

"Expect the stock market and foreign investments to go down, and business to be slower than usual as the public begins to comprehend that the developments in the Senate are not just political but more of a business move," a business executive who declined to be identified told Reuters.

The legislators who took part in Thursday's coup against Senate president Neptali Gonzales said their move was aimed at uniting the opposition, particularly against efforts to amend the constitution and extend the term of President Fidel Ramos.
But some Manila newspapers saw more to the plot, alleging it was backed by businessmen Eduardo Cojuangco and Lucio Tan, both close associates of the late President Ferdinand Marcos.

The Today newspaper reported that Cojuangco had advised opposition senators to unite to stop Ramos's supporters from changing the constitution and cancelling the 1998 presidential election. Tan's role was not spelt out.
Gonzales's replacement, Senator Enresto Maceda, was also closely linked with Marcos.
"The latest coup appears to signal the return of the Marcos boys," The Manila Times said in an editorial.
Philippine politics, however, are full of people once associated with the government overthrown in 1986. Ramos himself was the head of the paramilitary Philippine Constabulary under Marcos.

Despite Ramos's repeated statements that he is not interested in going beyond the single six-year term the constitution allows, members of his Lakas party are gathering signatures for a petition that could set in motion a process to amend the charter.

Economists credit Ramos with masterminding the revival of the Philippine economy, which was at a virtual standstill when he took office in 1992 but is expected to grow by 6.5 to 7.5 percent this year.
Political analyst Alex Magno said the changing of the Senate guard could hold back foreign investment.
"It's normal after a major political event for investors to hold back and figure out what's happening," Magno said in a telephone interview.
Investors would be worried that the Senate coup would jeopardise passage of crucial government tax reforms.

News of Gonzales' ouster sent Manila stocks tumbling, with the main index dropping 55.13 points at midsession, brokers said. The index later regained some ground but closed at 2,973.59, down 28.76 points on the day.
The local stock market has been taking a battering all week led by foreign selling. The index started the week at 3,131.

Gonzales himself, however, indicated there was nothing sinister in his own downfall but that it was all part of normal Philippine political life, where loyalties are fluid and horse-trading continuous.
"It's a game of musical chairs," he told reporters.
